top.h1: Leonardo da Vinci's life, year by year
top.answer: Leonardo da Vinci was a painter and engineer. He painted the Mona Lisa and the Last Supper. He was born near Vinci in Tuscany on 15 April 1452, the day his grandfather wrote down, and he died at Cloux, by Amboise in France, on 2 May 1519, aged 67. Here is his life year by year, and every dated line says how sure it is.

paras: Every dated line below carries the mark the museum's timeline gives it. Documented means a record from the time names the date: a contract, a letter, a tax return, a note in his own hand. Inferred means scholars work it out from such records, and tradition means a story told later, with no record behind it.

blocks.intro: His life in seven parts, as the museum's timeline tells it. The seventh begins after his death.

periods.p: We know the day and the hour of his birth because his grandfather Antonio wrote them into an old notarial register, a note that turned up in the state archive in Florence and was printed in 1939. The note names no place, so the farmhouse at Anchiano that is shown today as his birthplace has only tradition behind it. He grew up in Vinci with his father's family, and as a son born outside marriage he could not become a notary like his father, ser Piero. His teacher was Andrea del Verrocchio, in Florence. His first big commissions, an altarpiece and the Adoration of the Magi, both stayed unfinished.

items.line: He is born at the third hour of night, close to 10 pm by today's clock. His grandfather Antonio notes the day, the hour and the name, Lionardo.
He trains in Verrocchio's workshop in Florence. No apprenticeship contract survives. The museum's timeline puts the start at about 1466, other scholars earlier.
A Florentine household declaration lists him as ser Piero's son, born outside marriage, aged seventeen.
His name enters the book of Florence's painters' company.
He dates a drawing of the Arno valley. It is the earliest drawing with a date in his hand.
An anonymous accusation of sodomy names him and three other men. It also places him with Verrocchio. An accusation is not a finding of guilt.
The renewed charge is dismissed, and all the accused are absolved.
Florence's government, the Signoria, orders an altarpiece from him. The sources disagree on the day.
The monks of San Donato order the Adoration of the Magi from him. His father is their notary. Sources differ on the month and on his deadline.

links.text: See the pictures of his Florence years in the wing

periods.p: About 1482, at around thirty, he probably moved to Milan, to the court of Ludovico Sforza, called il Moro, who ruled the city and became its duke in 1494. An early writer says Lorenzo de' Medici sent him there with a lyre. For about seventeen years he worked in Milan: a model for the cathedral's tower, festivals for the court, a giant clay horse for a bronze statue, and the Last Supper. His household grew: in 1493 Caterina, whom scholars usually take for his mother, joined it. In 1499 the French took Milan and Ludovico fled. Leonardo sent 600 gold florins to his account in Florence and left by December with Luca Pacioli, for Mantua and Venice.

items.line: An undated draft letter, corrected in his own hand, offers Ludovico Sforza his services as an engineer and artist.
He and the de Predis brothers sign the Virgin of the Rocks contract. It is the first hard record of him in Milan.
Milan cathedral's accounts record work on a model for its crossing tower.
Giacomo, a boy of ten, comes to live in his household. Later he is called Salaì.
The clay model of the great horse is shown at a Sforza wedding.
Ludovico sends the bronze meant for the horse to be made into cannon.
The court presses him to finish the Last Supper.
Luca Pacioli, in the dedication of his book De divina proportione, describes the Last Supper as finished.
Ludovico gives him a vineyard outside the Porta Vercellina.
A later writer, Sabba da Castiglione, says Gascon crossbowmen used the clay horse as a target.

periods.h: Venice, Florence and the Romagna, 1500 to 1506
periods.p: From Mantua, where he drew Isabella d'Este, he went on to Venice, where a letter of 13 March 1500 places him, and by April he was back in Florence. In Venice he gave advice on defending the city against the Turks. In Florence a letter of 1501 found him busy with geometry and out of patience with the brush. For Cesare Borgia he surveyed fortresses in the Romagna. Back in Florence in 1503 he began the portrait of Lisa del Giocondo and took on the Battle of Anghiari, a wall painting for the hall of the Great Council. On 30 May 1506 he left for Milan, promising to be back within three months, and his stay there lasted far longer.

items.line: Cesare Borgia names him architect and general engineer.
He draws his plan of the town of Imola, which survives at Windsor. Scholars usually date it to that autumn.
Agostino Vespucci writes a dated note in the margin of a book. It names Leonardo's portrait of Lisa del Giocondo and a Saint Anne.
The contract for the Battle of Anghiari records a payment. It sets a deadline for the cartoon, the full-size drawing.
He writes down his father's death. Two editors of his notes read the day differently.

links.text: See the Mona Lisa in the wing
The Mona Lisa: who she was, and how she was stolen in 1911

periods.p: Milan was French now, governed by Charles d'Amboise. In 1507 King Louis XII called him his own painter and engineer. From about August 1507 to the spring of 1508 he was back in Florence, in a quarrel with his half-brothers over his uncle Francesco's will, and studied anatomy at Santa Maria Nuova. Back in Milan he filled his notes with studies of water and the earth. In these years a young Milanese nobleman, Francesco Melzi, became his pupil. After Charles d'Amboise died, Leonardo stayed from 1511 at the Melzi villa at Vaprio d'Adda.

items.line: Charles d'Amboise, the French governor of Milan, asks Florence to let him remain in Milan for two months.
He works out plans for a horse and rider monument for Trivulzio.
His studies of anatomy run through these years. Vasari, writing later, names della Torre as his partner in them.

links.text: See his anatomy sheets in the wing

periods.p: Giuliano de' Medici, the brother of Pope Leo X, was his patron in Rome and gave him rooms in the Belvedere of the Vatican. Leonardo worked on mirrors, on geometry and on plans for the Pontine marshes, but the records of these years are thin. Giuliano died in March 1516, and that year Leonardo left for France.

items.line: He notes his departure for Rome with Melzi, Salaì, Lorenzo and il Fanfoia.
Later writers describe a mechanical lion for a royal entry. Where and for which occasion is uncertain.

links.text: The mechanical lion, and what the old accounts say

p: In France he lived at Cloux, today the Clos Lucé, close to the royal castle of Amboise. Melzi came with him. His last years in France, his will, his death and his grave have

items.line: He enters the service of King Francis I and lives at Cloux.
A cardinal's secretary notes a visit and three paintings. Leonardo's right hand is partly paralysed, he writes, yet he still draws and teaches.
He dies at Cloux, aged 67. Melzi reports the death in a letter of 1 June.

links.text: See his last house in the wing

periods.p: Melzi inherited his books and notes. Thousands of pages of his notes survive, and you can turn some of them at the wing's reading table.

items.line: After Melzi's death the manuscripts pass to his son Orazio.
The sculptor Pompeo Leoni buys sheets and binds them into new albums.
Arconati gives the Codex Atlanticus, the largest gathering of his sheets, and other manuscripts to the Ambrosiana, a library in Milan.
French requisitions take the manuscripts to Paris.
The Codex Atlanticus returns to Milan. The smaller manuscripts stay in Paris.
The Mona Lisa is stolen from the Louvre.
The stolen Mona Lisa is found again in Florence.

blocks.h: What people ask about his life

items.a: No marriage of his is known. No document of his life names a wife.
items.known: His will, made at Cloux in April 1519, leaves his books and drawings to his pupil Melzi and remembers Salaì, two servants and his half-brothers. It names no wife and no child, and no other record read for this page names one. That tells us what the records lack, not whom he loved.

items.q: Did Leonardo da Vinci have children?
items.a: No child of his is known.
items.known: No record names a son or a daughter of his, and his will mentions none. The young men who lived in his house, Salaì and later Melzi, were his pupils and helpers, not his children.

items.a: No document settles it. The records hold one case from 1476, and it ended with the accused absolved. No wife or child of his is known. For many years he shared a household with Salaì, and later with Melzi.
items.known: In Florence in April 1476, an unsigned denunciation named him, with three other men, in a case of sodomy. The charge was dropped, the case ended in June with the accused absolved, and an accusation is not a finding of guilt. Several scholars, among them Frank Zöllner and Giovanni Dall'Orto, read him as a man who loved men. The historian Elizabeth Abbott thinks he would likely count as gay in today's words, but chose a celibate life after 1476, and points out that being gay, as an identity, was not an idea of his time. A few others have searched for a woman in his life, on very weak evidence, and Sigmund Freud's famous reading of 1910 rested on a mistranslated word. No document settles it either way.

items.q: Who were Leonardo da Vinci's parents?
items.a: His father was ser Piero da Vinci, a notary in Florence. His mother was a woman named Caterina, and the two were not married.
items.known: His grandfather's tax return from the late 1450s lists the boy as ser Piero's son, not born in marriage, and names his mother Caterina, by then the wife of a man of Vinci known as Accattabriga. Who she was is still argued over. In 2023 the scholar Carlo Vecce presented a deed that Leonardo's father wrote in November 1452, freeing an enslaved woman named Caterina from the Caucasus, and Vecce thinks she was Leonardo's mother. Martin Kemp and Giuseppe Pallanti argued in 2017 for a poor orphan from near Vinci. Both are hypotheses, and no document says which, if either, is right. In 1493 a Caterina moved into his house in Milan, and about a year later he paid for her funeral: scholars usually take her to be his mother.

items.q: Did Leonardo da Vinci have siblings?
items.a: No full brothers or sisters are known, but he had many half-siblings. When his father died in 1504, eleven more of his father's children were living, and his mother had five children with her husband.
items.known: Ser Piero had four wives, one after another, and his first child in marriage came only in 1476, when Leonardo was 24. At his father's death Leonardo noted two daughters and ten sons, himself among the sons, so nine half-brothers and two half-sisters were living. Counting children who died young, Museo Galileo gives at least sixteen. His mother had four daughters and a son with Accattabriga. In 1507 Leonardo quarrelled with his half-brothers over the will of his uncle Francesco.

items.a: Two young men of his household. Salaì came to him as a boy of ten in 1490 and stayed about 25 years, and Francesco Melzi, a young Milanese nobleman, became his pupil and his heir.
items.known: Salaì's real name was Gian Giacomo Caprotti, from Oreno near Milan. In the note on his arrival Leonardo also listed the boy's thefts and called him a thief, a liar, stubborn and a glutton. The nickname Salaì comes from a devil in Pulci's poem Morgante. Melzi joined him during his second stay in Milan, went with him to Rome and France, wrote the letter that reported his death, and inherited his books and drawings.

items.a: Yes. He wrote his notes with his left hand, from right to left, so they read normally in a mirror.
items.known: Vasari already said so in 1568. In 2019 a study of his drawing dated 1473, by the Opificio delle Pietre Dure in Florence, found the date in mirror writing on the front, probably made with the left hand, and a line in ordinary script on the back, made with the right. So he could write both ways. Why he chose mirror writing is not known. The popular idea is that he did it to hide his ideas. We know of no record from his time that says so.

items.a: Nobody knows. The story rests on one comparison in one letter, and his own household accounts list meat.
items.known: Andrea Corsali, a Florentine travelling in India, wrote to Giuliano de' Medici about people there who eat nothing that has blood in it and harm no living thing, and compared them to “our Leonardo da Vinci”. The vegetarian story rests on that one comparison and nothing more. Museo Galileo points out that his lists of expenses often include meat, though it may have been for his household. Vasari, writing decades later, says he bought caged birds to let them fly off.

items.q: How tall was Leonardo da Vinci?
items.a: Nobody knows. No record gives his height.
items.known: Vasari, who wrote after his death, praises his good looks and his great strength, but gives no measure. The one portrait drawn from life that scholars generally accept is a profile in red chalk by Melzi, made about 1510 and kept at Windsor.

items.q: Did Leonardo da Vinci go to school?
items.a: Not to a Latin school. His schooling was in reckoning, the arithmetic of trade, and much of the rest he taught himself.
items.known: Vasari says he learned the abacus, as commercial arithmetic was called, and mastered it in a few months. In his own words he was a man without letters, meaning without Latin learning, and he wrote in Italian. In Milan, as a grown man, he worked through Latin grammar on his own.

blocks.intro: The page relies on the documents of his life as scholars have published them, from his grandfather's note to the records of 1476 in the Florence state archive, on his own notes in J. P. Richter's edition of 1883, Vasari's Life of Leonardo of 1568, Gustavo Uzielli's research of 1872 and 1896, the Treccani biographical dictionary, the chronology and pages of Museo Galileo in Florence, the Museo Leonardiano in Vinci, the Opificio delle Pietre Dure's 2019 study of his drawing of 1473 in the Uffizi, Walter Isaacson's biography of 2017, Live Science and Finestre sull'Arte, Carleton University's report on a lecture by Elizabeth Abbott, and the timeline of the museum's Leonardo wing, all read on 17 October 2026.
